evidence.paraphrase: An unnamed Brahmin sage of the Āṅgirasa family has Bharata as son. Fearful of attachment even in this birth, Bharata meditates on Gaṇeśa near the sage. Hearing Vedic and other Gaṇeśa praise strengthens previous knowledge. He conceals all cleverness, displaying dull childlike conduct out of fear of marriage and attachment. The father is an unnamed Āṅgirasa descendant, not the creator sage Aṅgiras himself.

evidence.verification_notes: Read actual cited body; attributed dialogue kept distinct from narrator fact. Independent root review pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Father gives Bharata sacred thread and teaches sandhyā, cleanliness and Vedic acts including ācamana. Bharata does not accept instruction, acts differently even when struck, performs acts when physically guided but later appears unable to recall them. People call him Jaḍa and doubt his knowledge; he disregards honor, insult, blame and praise. Father does not arrange marriage because of apparent dullness, which pleases Bharata.
evidence.verifier: Mudgala continuation6 author, direct Sanskrit body
evidence.verification_notes: Read actual cited body; attributed dialogue kept distinct from narrator fact. Independent root review pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Father dies in time; unnamed virtuous mother follows him (sahagā). Nine brothers born to his mother’s co-wife take control over Bharata: these are half-brothers in this later birth, not Ṛṣabha’s earlier sons. Their arrogant wives give leftovers, spoiled or burnt food and husks without affection. Brothers dishonor him with words/clothes and call him family disgrace. He eats rejected food as nectar wearing rags; when women withhold even that, he eats only once within two or three days. This is deprivation, not a fasting vow.
evidence.verifier: Mudgala continuation6 author, direct Sanskrit body
evidence.verification_notes: Read actual cited body; attributed dialogue kept distinct from narrator fact. Independent root review pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Hungry Bharata wanders house to house seeking food and accepts work. Pleased people give food/clothes; his brothers see him, bring him back and make him their worker. Their wives still give bad food/husks, which he eats as nectar. Brothers station him to guard ripe grain fields day and night for food; understanding bodily life, he remains equal in pleasure and pain.

evidence.paraphrase: Robber chief praises Bhadrakālī and promises a human victim if he obtains abundant wealth. Wealth is then actually obtained; source does not explicitly narrate a deity boon or identify its grantor. He sends robbers at night; they happen upon Bharata, seize him by force and take him to their station. Bharata understands bodily prārabdha. Chief honors and feeds him tasty food, then takes him with music to the goddess.

evidence.paraphrase: After Mahākālī worship the chief draws a naked sword to kill Bharata. Seeing possible bodily death, Bharata is unshaken and remembers Gaṇapati, accepting whether body falls today or lives long. Angry Gaṇapatya Mahākālī emerges from the image, takes the chief’s sword from his hand, beheads him with it and drinks blood. Other robbers are killed with that sword. Goddess plays with her own gaṇas while intent on Gaṇeśa praise. Bharata bows and leaves, wandering freely for alms while remembering Gaṇapati. No actual liberation narrated.

evidence.paraphrase: Sindhu ruler Rahūgaṇa is inwardly inclined through prior saṃskāra but cannot gain peace despite effort. He goes toward Kapila’s āśrama near Gaṅgā, said by a Brahmin to be on Gautamī’s south bank. His palanquin bearers tire; attendants recruit replacements, finding the Āṅgirasa sage Bharata. Accepting bodily prārabdha he carries without distress. To avoid injuring creatures he steps only where none are present, slowing bearers and rocking the palanquin, distressing king. Gaṅgā/Gautamī labels preserved as this witness’s setting, not mapped to modern geography.
evidence.verifier: Mudgala continuation6 author, direct Sanskrit body
evidence.verification_notes: Read actual cited body; attributed dialogue kept distinct from narrator fact. Independent root review pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Angry Rahūgaṇa orders steady carrying; fearful bearers blame newcomer as moving like drunk. King rebukes him as wicked/mad. Knowing king desires yoga and is qualified, Bharata replies that all is māyā/delusion/untrue, questions king/people division, says he has abandoned duality/equality and king cannot discipline him into abandoning yoga. He resumes silently carrying and worshipping Gaṇapati. Hearing yogic speech, frightened king jumps to ground, sees ragged Brahmin with sacred thread/Brahman radiance, prostrates and addresses him respectfully.

evidence.paraphrase: Rahūgaṇa explains fear of offending Brahmins: he praises them as Supreme Lord’s bodies, supports of acts/knowledge/Brahman, their mouths convey offerings to gods, gifts yield imperishable state, mantras/gods depend on them and mantra-less acts are fruitless. He calls devoted act/tapas/knowledge/yoga Brahmins liberators/teachers/Brahman. He attributes divine falls to slighting/curses, restoration to Brahmins and all attainment to service. He fears them more than Viṣṇu/Śiva. Taking Bharata’s feet, bowing with head there, he cries; compassionate Bharata raises him and begins reply. These claims are king’s praise, not universal physical/social facts or new narrated curses.
